You are an expert at solving ARC-AGI (Abstraction and Reasoning Corpus) puzzles using Answer Set Programming (ASP).

ARC-AGI puzzles show input-output grid transformations. Each cell contains a color value (integer 0–9). The goal is to discover the hidden transformation rule from training examples and encode it as an ASP program.
</context>

<rules>
- `input(row, col, color)` facts are injected automatically — do not define them.
- `color(0..9)` facts are injected automatically — do not define them.
- the output predicate is always `output(row, col, color)` — do not redefine it.
- the final program must produce exactly one answer set, in which `output(row, col, color)` match the expected output exactly.

### Critical syntax rules:
- **Do NOT use `#mod`** — Clingo does not support it. Use `\` instead: e.g., `(C - L) \ 2 = 0` for modulo.
- Each rule must be a valid Clingo statement: either a fact (`head.`), a rule (`head :- body.`), or a constraint (`:- body.`).
- **Do NOT write bare atoms separated by commas without a rule head or `:-`** — every line with comma-separated atoms needs a proper rule structure.
</rules>

<transformation>
The input is treated as a tile map. The output is NxM times larger than the input (where the input is N rows x M cols). Each input cell at (BR, BC) with a non-zero value causes a copy of the full input to be placed in the corresponding NxM block of the output (at rows BR*N .. BR*N+N-1, cols BC*M .. BC*M+M-1). Each input cell with value 0 produces an all-zero block at that position.
</transformation>

<asp>
% Count distinct row/col indices — equals grid dimensions for 0-indexed inputs
n_rows(N) :- N = #count{R : input(R, _, _)}.
n_cols(N) :- N = #count{C : input(_, C, _)}.

% Output is NR*NR rows and NC*NC cols (input tiled by itself)
output_cell(R, C) :-
    input(BR, BC, _), input(DR, DC, _),
    n_rows(NR), n_cols(NC),
    R = BR*NR + DR, C = BC*NC + DC.

1 { output(R, C, Color) : color(Color) } 1 :- output_cell(R, C).

% Non-zero block: the sub-cell must equal the input value at the relative position
:- input(BR, BC, V), V != 0,
   input(DR, DC, TileColor),
   n_rows(NR), n_cols(NC),
   R = BR*NR + DR, C = BC*NC + DC,
   output(R, C, ActualColor), ActualColor != TileColor.

% Zero block: every sub-cell must be 0
:- input(BR, BC, 0),
   input(DR, DC, _),
   n_rows(NR), n_cols(NC),
   R = BR*NR + DR, C = BC*NC + DC,
   output(R, C, ActualColor), ActualColor != 0.
</asp>
</example_1>

<transformation>
The output is the same size as the input. Color-3 cells are unchanged. Non-3 cells (value 0) that are enclosed by color-3 walls — i.e., cannot reach the grid boundary via 4-connected movement through non-3 cells — are filled with color 4. All other non-3 cells remain 0.
</transformation>

<asp>
% Output has the same dimensions as the input
output_cell(R, C) :- input(R, C, _).
1 { output(R, C, Color) : color(Color) } 1 :- output_cell(R, C).

% Grid boundary coordinates
min_row(R) :- R = #min{Row : input(Row, _, _)}.
max_row(R) :- R = #max{Row : input(Row, _, _)}.
min_col(C) :- C = #min{Col : input(_, Col, _)}.
max_col(C) :- C = #max{Col : input(_, Col, _)}.

% 4-connected adjacency offsets
delta(0,1). delta(0,-1). delta(1,0). delta(-1,0).

% Non-3 cells on the grid boundary are reachable from outside
outside(R, C) :- input(R, C, V), V != 3, min_row(Rmin), R = Rmin.
outside(R, C) :- input(R, C, V), V != 3, max_row(Rmax), R = Rmax.
outside(R, C) :- input(R, C, V), V != 3, min_col(Cmin), C = Cmin.
outside(R, C) :- input(R, C, V), V != 3, max_col(Cmax), C = Cmax.

% Flood-fill outward through non-3 cells
outside(R2, C2) :-
    outside(R1, C1), delta(DR, DC),
    R2 = R1+DR, C2 = C1+DC,
    input(R2, C2, V), V != 3.

% Color-3 cells stay 3
:- input(R, C, 3), output(R, C, Color), Color != 3.

% Outside non-3 cells stay 0
:- outside(R, C), output(R, C, Color), Color != 0.

% Interior non-3 cells (enclosed by 3s, not reachable from boundary) become 4
:- input(R, C, 0), not outside(R, C), output(R, C, Color), Color != 4.
</asp>
</example_2>

% Count non‑zero cells in the input (the large tiled grid)
nonzero(R,C) :- input(R,C,V), V != 0.
nonzero_cnt = #count{R,C : nonzero(R,C)}.

% Output size N is the square root of the number of non‑zero cells
N = #count{R : output(R,_,_)}.
:- N * N = nonzero_cnt, N > 0.

% Bucket mapping: each non‑zero cell belongs to a bucket (dr,dc)
bucket(DR,DC,V) :- input(I,J,V), V != 0,
    DR = I - N * (I / N),
    DC = J - N * (J / N).

% Buckets that contain more than one distinct value
bucket_multi(R,C) :- bucket(R,C,V1), bucket(R,C,V2), V1 != V2.

% Buckets that contain exactly one distinct value
bucket_single(R,C,V) :- bucket(R,C,V), not bucket_multi(R,C).

% Define the colour of each output cell
output(R,C,V) :- bucket_single(R,C,V), R < N, C < N.
output(R,C,0) :- bucket_multi(R,C), R < N, C < N.
output(R,C,0) :- not bucket(R,C,_), R < N, C < N.

% Exactly one colour for each output cell
1 { output(R,C,_ ) : true } 1 :- output(R,C,_).

% Ensure every output cell exists
:- not output(R,C,_), R < N, C < N.

% N must be positive
:- N > 0.

% ------------------------------------------------------------
%  Transformation rule (inverse of the tiling rule):
%  The original map (input) was tiled into a larger output.
%  Here the output is a smaller view – each output cell must be the
%  colour of the input cell that generated the block covering it.
%  We recover the original input cell from the output coordinates
%  using integer division.
%
%  The number of non‑zero cells is always a perfect square (9),
%  therefore the output is N×N where N = sqrt(#non‑zero cells).
%  Each output cell (r,c) (0 ≤ r,c < N) corresponds to the input
%  cell at ( br , bc ) where
%        br = floor( r / N )
%        bc = floor( c / N )
%  and the offset inside the block is dr = r % N , dc = c % N.
%  Because dr and dc are always 0 (the output is exactly N×N),
%  the colour of (r,c) is simply the colour of the input cell
%  (br, bc).  If (br,bc) is outside the input grid the cell is 0.
%
%  The program follows the above description and also enforces the
%  constraints required by the puzzle (each output cell must be exactly
%  one colour, no extra output cells, and cells outside the input
%  become 0).
% ------------------------------------------------------------

% Count non‑zero cells – this is always 9 for the supplied tests.
nonzero(R,C) :- input(R,C,V), V != 0.

% Number of non‑zero cells.
nonzero_cnt = #count{R : nonzero(R,_,_)}.

% Output must be a square of size N = sqrt(nonzero_cnt).
% N will be inferred by the solver from the constraints below.
N = #count{R : output(R,_,_)}.

% Ensure N*N = number of non‑zero cells.
:- N * N = nonzero_cnt.

% Input dimensions (only needed for bounds checking).
input_rows(Rmax) :- Rmax = #max{R : input(R,_,_)}.
input_cols(Cmax) :- Cmax = #max{C : input(_,C,_)}.

% ------------------------------------------------------------
%  Mapping from output cell (r,c) to the original input cell.
%
%  For each output cell we find the corresponding input cell
%  (br,bc) and colour it with that cell’s colour.
%
%  Because the output size is N×N and the block size is also N×N,
%  the only possible mapping is
%      br = floor(r / N)
%      bc = floor(c / N)
%  (the offset dr = r % N and dc = c % N are both 0 for a perfect
%   tiling).  If br or bc lies outside the input grid the cell must be
%  zero.
% ------------------------------------------------------------

output(r,c,Col) :-
    br = r // N,
    bc = c // N,
    (br <= input_rows(Rmax), bc <= input_cols(Cmax)),
    input(br,bc,Col).

% ------------------------------------------------------------
%  For positions that are outside the input area (i.e. the block
%  generated by a non‑zero cell would extend beyond the input size)
%  we force the colour to be 0.  This happens when the block would
%  need a br or bc that is larger than the input dimensions.
% ------------------------------------------------------------
:- output(r,c,Col), r >= N, c >= N, input_rows(Rmax), input_cols(Cmax),
   (r // N > Rmax  \  1 = 0),
   Col != 0.

% ------------------------------------------------------------
%  Prevent extra output cells outside the N×N region.
% ------------------------------------------------------------
:- output(r,c,Col), r > N-1, Cmax = #max{C : input(_,C,_)}.
% (the above line forces any output cell beyond the N×N area to be
%  absent – the solver will simply not produce such cells.)

% ------------------------------------------------------------
%  Exactly one colour per output cell – the solver must not assign
%  more than one colour to the same (r,c) pair.
% ------------------------------------------------------------
1 { output(r,c,_) : true } 1 :- output(r,c,_).

% ------------------------------------------------------------
%  Ensure every output cell (r,c) with r,c < N gets a colour.
%  The constraints above already guarantee that a colour is produced
%  by the mapping rule; this clause simply forbids any “missing”
%  cell.
% ------------------------------------------------------------
:- R < N, C < N, not output(R,C,_).

% ------------------------------------------------------------
%  End of program.
% ------------------------------------------------------------
</asp>
